opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because I think the field has spent a lot of time looking at quality in isolation, and in practice nobody deploys a model in isolation. You're always making a trade-off.

On the quality side, we look at the standard benchmarks people care about: coding, math and reasoning, general knowledge and instruction following. But I try not to over-index on any single leaderboard number. A lot of what matters is whether the model is good enough for the task the customer actually has. For many real applications, like code completion, editing, agentic workflows, or customer support, you hit a quality threshold where the model is plenty capable. After that, the questions that matter are how fast it is and how much it costs to serve.

So I think of it as a frontier. You can plot quality against latency or throughput, and against cost per token, and ask where a given model sits on that curve. What we've been trying to do with diffusion-based language models is push that frontier out. If you can match the quality of an autoregressive model of a similar class while generating tokens many times faster, because you're producing them in parallel and refining them rather than one at a time, you're also getting much better GPU utilization. That translates directly into lower cost per query.

Speed also matters more than people tend to think. It isn't just a nice-to-have. In agentic settings a model might call itself dozens or hundreds of times, and in interactive settings like coding a developer is waiting on the output. Latency compounds, and it changes what's feasible to build at all. A system that's ten times faster lets you do more test-time computation for the same budget, like more sampling, more verification, and more iterations. That can feed back into quality.

So my short answer is that we measure all three together, and we try to evaluate on the workloads people actually run rather than only on academic benchmarks. The goal is the best quality you can get at a given latency and cost point, not the best quality at any price.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes quality, latency, and cost as a trade-off and says to measure all three together.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark limitations and practical quality thresholds, but does not say quality is harder to measure than speed or cost.

r003.rationale: It names standard benchmarks for coding, math and reasoning, general knowledge, and instruction following as ways to assess quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that you can't really separate them anymore. For a long time the field treated quality as the thing you optimize and speed and cost as afterthoughts, something the infrastructure people deal with later. But if you look at what actually gets deployed, the question is always: what's the best quality I can get at a given latency and a given price point? That's a Pareto frontier, not a single number.

So the way I think about it is, first, quality has to be measured on the task you actually care about. Benchmarks like MMLU or the standard coding evals are useful as a sanity check, but they saturate, and they don't tell you much about whether the model is going to hold up on your workload. We spend a lot of time building task-specific evals, often with real user prompts, and we look at things like win rates against a reference model rather than a single accuracy number.

Then speed. People usually mean tokens per second, but that's not quite right either. What matters to a user is time to first token and time to a usable answer. And this is where the architecture starts to matter a lot. Autoregressive models have this fundamental constraint that they generate one token at a time, so your latency scales with output length no matter how clever your serving stack is. That's a big part of why we got interested in diffusion-based language models at Inception. If you can generate tokens in parallel and refine them, you change the shape of the tradeoff. You're not just moving along the curve, you're moving the curve.

And then cost is really the same thing viewed from the provider's side. Fewer forward passes per output means fewer GPU-seconds, which means you can either charge less or serve more users on the same hardware. So speed and cost are deeply coupled, and both of them trade against quality.

The practical thing I'd tell people is: don't evaluate quality in isolation and then ask whether it's fast enough. Fix the latency and cost budget that your application actually has, and then ask what the best quality is inside that budget. A model that's two points better on a benchmark but three times slower is usually worse for the product. And there's a whole class of applications, like real-time coding assistants, agents that take many steps, voice interfaces, where the latency constraint is so tight that the question of quality only makes sense once you've met it.

r001.rationale: The response says quality, speed, and cost trade against one another and frames the goal as maximizing quality within latency and price limits.

r002.rationale: It says quality depends on the task and that general benchmarks can be limited, but does not state that quality is harder to measure than speed or cost.

r003.rationale: It mentions established benchmarks as sanity checks, but says they saturate and may not reflect a user's workload. It does not describe them as representing capabilities users care about.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at these together, because quality depends on what you’re trying to do. A model can perform very well on a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how useful it will be for your application. Can it solve the tasks you care about? How often does it make mistakes, and how costly are those mistakes?

Then you want to measure that quality alongside latency and cost under comparable conditions. If you give one model more time or more computation, it may produce a better answer. So rather than looking for a single best model, I’d look at the tradeoff: what quality can you achieve within a particular budget? For an interactive application, response time might be a hard constraint. For a difficult problem where you can wait, spending more computation could be worthwhile.

r001.rationale: It explicitly recommends weighing quality against latency and cost, including what quality can be achieved within a budget.

r002.rationale: It says quality depends on the task and that benchmarks may not predict usefulness, but does not state that quality is harder to measure than speed or cost.

r003.rationale: It mentions benchmark performance, then cautions that a benchmark may not reflect application usefulness. It does not describe using established benchmarks that represent capabilities users care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at the tradeoff among all three. A model might produce excellent answers, but if it takes too long or costs too much, it may not be useful for your application. And a very fast, cheap model isn’t useful if it doesn’t meet your quality requirements.

So I would start with the task: what does a good answer look like, and how reliably do you need to produce it? Then you can compare approaches at a fixed quality level and ask how much time and computation they require. You also want to measure the whole system. If a cheaper model needs multiple attempts or a lot of verification, that can change the cost and latency substantially.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes a trade-off among quality, speed, and cost.

r002.rationale: It does not state that quality is harder to measure than speed or cost.

r003.rationale: It does not mention established benchmarks or measuring performance on them.
